title: Practice in the dark
hook: a lamp blows out at dinner and Arjuna learns what practice does; abhyasa, and the breath routine built this week
carry: abhyasa is practice that works in the dark
tomorrow: a little girl asks who her groom will be. the answer is a god.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Panchajanya, the conch from the sea. Your line was the conch is breath offered as holy sound. Today breath week ends, with a prince eating dinner in the dark.
screen: `THE CONCH IS BREATH OFFERED AS HOLY SOUND.`

segments.voice: In the Mahabharata, the young princes are learning archery from their teacher Drona, and Arjuna is the keenest of them all. One night he's eating dinner when a gust of wind blows out the lamp. Total dark. And Arjuna notices something. His hand still finds his mouth. Every bite. He doesn't need to see. Years of doing it every day have taught his hand the way.
screen: `A PRINCE AT DINNER.` → `THE LAMP BLOWS OUT.` → `HIS HAND STILL KNOWS THE WAY.`

segments.voice: So Arjuna starts practicing archery at night, in the dark. Drona hears a bowstring twanging after everyone's asleep, goes out, finds him, embraces him, and promises to make him an archer without equal. Later in the same epic, Krishna gives the idea its name. You heard it on day ninety-eight: Arjuna complains that the mind is as restless as the wind, and Krishna says it can still be held, by abhyasa, practice, and by letting go. Abhyasa means steady practice, again and again, over a long time. It's one of Hinduism's most practical teachings: the mind isn't changed in one big moment, but by small repetitions, until it knows the way in the dark. It's why so many Hindus keep a daily practice: a lamp at the shrine, a few minutes of prayer, a few minutes of breath. This week built yours. The word for that breath work is pranayama: prana, breath and life, and ayama, lengthening; some read it as yama, restraint. In the classic picture of yoga it's the fourth of eight steps, after how you treat others, how you live, and how you sit. Here's your five minutes. Watch the breath for thirty seconds. Four in, six out, for a minute. A soft two-count pause, only if it's comfortable. Five rounds of alternate nostrils. Three long hums. A minute of ujjayi, then let it fade, and sit. On a rushed morning, two pieces is still the practice. What matters is coming back.
screen: `ARJUNA PRACTICES IN THE DARK.` · `ABHYASA: PRACTICE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `SMALL REPETITIONS, EVERY DAY.` · `PRANAYAMA: THE FOURTH OF EIGHT STEPS.` · then, large: `ABHYASA IS PRACTICE THAT WORKS IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Here's the short version, to fit the time: watch three breaths just as they are, then four in, six out, three times, then three rounds of alternate nostrils. One long hum, mmm, and then, mouth closed, a few soft ocean breaths. Then let it all go and just sit, the way Arjuna's hand found the way without looking.
Pranayama. Prana, breath and life; ayama, lengthening. The practice of the breath, the fourth step of yoga.
Hold on to it: abhyasa is practice that works in the dark. Breath week is done, and the routine is yours. Day one hundred three.

chat.meaning: Arjuna's hand found his mouth in the dark because of daily practice. Krishna calls it abhyasa: the mind is trained by steady repetition, which is why so many Hindus keep the same small practice every day.
